# Introduction

Missing protein intensities can follow more than one pattern. Some values are
absent for approximately intensity-independent, MAR-like reasons. Low-abundance
features can instead fall below detection and produce MNAR-like missingness. A
protein can also be present throughout one condition and absent throughout
another. A single label across all samples can hide that on/off pattern.

ImputeFinder takes unnormalised log2 protein intensities, classifies each
feature separately within each condition, and removes features that lack enough
observations for the intended downstream branch. The result records each state,
cutoff, rescue value, and drop reason. The labels mean **likely MAR** and
**likely MNAR** under an intensity-cutoff rule; they do not establish the true
cause of missingness. ImputeFinder neither normalises nor imputes values.

Bioconductor packages such as
[`DEP`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/DEP),
[`MSnbase`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/MSnbase), and
[`msImpute`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/msImpute) provide broader
proteomics analysis or imputation machinery. ImputeFinder has a narrower role:
it preserves condition-specific state and coordinates separate downstream
branches while returning either an ordinary matrix or a
`SummarizedExperiment`.

Within a pipeline, those states can form an auditable routing layer. MNAR blocks
can enter a detection-limit branch, MAR blocks can enter a relationship-based
branch, and complete blocks can pass through unchanged.

# Installation

Once ImputeFinder is available from a Bioconductor package repository, install
and load it as follows. Installation code is intentionally not evaluated while
building the vignette.

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("imputefinder")

library(imputefinder)
```

# Inputs and classification rules

The input must be an ordinary numeric matrix, or a selected numeric assay in a
`SummarizedExperiment`, with named protein features in rows and uniquely named
samples in columns. Missing values are `NA`; `NaN` and infinite values are
rejected. Condition labels must align one-to-one with samples. ImputeFinder
trusts the scientific input contract: it does not infer or apply a log
transform, normalisation, centring, or scaling, and it does not reinterpret
zero.

After rescue, each feature-condition block receives exactly one state:

- `complete` - no value is missing.
- `MNAR` - at least one value is missing and the arithmetic mean of observed
    values is below the condition cutoff.
- `MAR` - at least one value is missing, the mean is at or above the cutoff,
    and strictly more than half the samples are observed.
- `insufficient` - the block is on the MAR side of the cutoff but lacks a
    strict observed majority.

The arithmetic mean is deliberate: one strong observation can move a partly
observed block toward the MAR side, and a mean equal to the cutoff is also on
that side. MAR-like downstream methods need relationships among observed
values, so a strict majority provides a minimum amount of within-condition
information. The majority rule applies only to MAR candidates. A sparse,
low-intensity block can remain MNAR because one observation may be the only
available evidence near the detection limit.

A feature is dropped if it is absent globally, `insufficient` in any condition,
or `MNAR` in every condition. Otherwise its complete state matrix is retained,
including mixtures such as MNAR in one condition and complete in another. An
`insufficient` block cannot support a MAR branch, while an all-MNAR feature has
no complete or MAR-like condition to support retention.

# Real-data example: K63-linked diubiquitin affinity enrichment

The [`DEP`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/DEP) package includes `DiUbi`, a
published ubiquitin-affinity proteomics dataset from
[Zhang et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.01.004). The full
experiment compares controls with several linkage-specific diubiquitin baits.

To make every classification state visible, this vignette embeds seven protein
rows from the three controls and three K63-linked samples. The values reproduce
the original MaxQuant `Intensity` columns archived under PRIDE accession
[PXD004185](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD004185). Zero entries
were converted to `NA`, and non-zero raw intensities were log2-transformed and
rounded to three decimals. No between-sample normalisation was applied. Both
manual cutoffs are 22.

```{r manual-fixture}
x <- rbind(
    VEGFA = c(NA, NA, NA, 22.850, 22.408, 22.795),
    UBE2I = c(22.135, 23.049, NA, 24.574, 24.966, 25.468),
    MED20 = c(24.193, 22.755, 23.093, NA, 20.445, 24.145),
    TXNRD1 = c(NA, NA, 22.639, NA, 17.848, 19.665),
    ATP11C = c(21.585, 20.692, NA, NA, NA, NA),
    UBA6 = rep(NA_real_, 6),
    ACO2 = c(26.351, 26.496, 27.103, 25.714, 25.753, 26.093)
)
sample_metadata <- data.frame(
    sample = c(paste0("control_", 1:3), paste0("K63_", 1:3)),
    condition = rep(c("control", "K63"), each = 3),
    replicate = rep(1:3, times = 2),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
colnames(x) <- sample_metadata$sample
condition <- sample_metadata$condition

fit <- classify_missingness(
    x,
    group = condition,
    cutoffs = c(control = 22, K63 = 22),
    seed = 1L
)
fit
```

```{r manual-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap=manual_heatmap_caption}
manual_heatmap <- data.frame(
    feature = rep(rownames(x), times = ncol(x)),
    sample = rep(colnames(x), each = nrow(x)),
    intensity = as.vector(x),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
manual_heatmap$feature <- factor(
    manual_heatmap$feature,
    levels = rev(rownames(x))
)
manual_heatmap$sample <- factor(
    manual_heatmap$sample,
    levels = colnames(x)
)
manual_heatmap$condition <- factor(
    sample_metadata$condition[
        match(as.character(manual_heatmap$sample), sample_metadata$sample)
    ],
    levels = c("control", "K63"),
    labels = c("Control", "K63-linked diubiquitin")
)
heatmap_sample_labels <- setNames(
    c(paste0("C", 1:3), paste0("K63-", 1:3)),
    colnames(x)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
    manual_heatmap,
    ggplot2::aes(x = sample, y = feature, fill = intensity)
) +
    ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.7) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
        data = manual_heatmap[is.na(manual_heatmap$intensity), , drop = FALSE],
        mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = sample, y = feature),
        inherit.aes = FALSE,
        shape = 4,
        size = 2.1,
        stroke = 0.7,
        colour = "#555555"
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_grid(
        cols = ggplot2::vars(condition),
        scales = "free_x",
        space = "free_x"
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = heatmap_sample_labels) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(
        low = "#F7FBFF",
        high = "#08519C",
        na.value = "#E0E0E0",
        name = "log2 intensity"
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Sample", y = "Protein") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
        panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(
            fill = "#F2F2F2",
            colour = NA
        ),
        strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9),
        legend.position = "right"
    )
```

Before classification, a feature missing everywhere is marked `all_missing`
and removed. Every surviving feature fully missing within one condition then
receives one artificial anchor:

1. The minimum finite intensity in each condition is calculated before any
    anchors are inserted.
2. One sample in each fully missing feature-condition block is selected
    uniformly. Selection is with replacement across features.
3. Exactly that cell receives the condition minimum; the others remain `NA`.
4. The feature, condition, selected sample, old and inserted values, and seed
    are recorded.

```{r rescue-log}
fit$seed_log
fit$data["VEGFA", ]
```

The anchor makes the absent condition classifiable; it is not a completed
imputation. Originally observed cells are preserved exactly. Stable name order
and a local RNG scope make the selected sample reproducible without changing
the global RNG state.

`feature_status` includes every original feature, including dropped rows. The
classification table contains the values used to assign each surviving
feature-condition state.

```{r classification-details}
fit$feature_status
fit$classifications[
    fit$classifications$feature %in%
        c("VEGFA", "MED20", "ATP11C"),
    c("feature", "condition", "observed_count", "missing_count",
        "mean_intensity", "cutoff", "state", "retained", "drop_reason")
]
```

```{r manual-state-map, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap=manual_state_caption}
state_features <- setdiff(rownames(x), "UBA6")
state_plot <- fit$classifications[
    fit$classifications$feature %in% state_features,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
]
state_plot$feature <- factor(
    state_plot$feature,
    levels = rev(state_features)
)
state_plot$condition <- factor(
    state_plot$condition,
    levels = c("control", "K63"),
    labels = c("Control", "K63-linked diubiquitin")
)
state_plot$state <- factor(
    state_plot$state,
    levels = c("complete", "MAR", "MNAR", "insufficient")
)
status_by_feature <- setNames(
    fit$feature_status$retained,
    fit$feature_status$feature
)
state_feature_labels <- setNames(
    ifelse(
        status_by_feature[state_features],
        state_features,
        paste0(state_features, " (filtered)")
    ),
    state_features
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
    state_plot,
    ggplot2::aes(x = condition, y = feature, fill = state)
) +
    ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.9) +
    ggplot2::geom_text(
        ggplot2::aes(label = state),
        size = 3.3,
        colour = "#222222"
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(labels = state_feature_labels) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
        values = c(
            complete = "#D9EAF7",
            MAR = "#DDECCB",
            MNAR = "#FBE3C3",
            insufficient = "#F2C9C9"
        ),
        drop = FALSE,
        name = "State"
    ) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Protein") +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
        panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom"
    )
```

# What pooling conditions would lose

The effect of pooling is easiest to see by applying the same cutoff and majority
rule to `VEGFA` as one block across all samples. In this extract, `VEGFA` is
absent from every control run and detected in every K63-linked run. The
comparison uses the original values, before condition-specific rescue.

```{r pooled-comparison}
pooled_values <- unname(x["VEGFA", ])
pooled_observed <- sum(!is.na(pooled_values))
pooled_mean <- mean(pooled_values, na.rm = TRUE)
pooled_state <- if (all(!is.na(pooled_values))) {
    "complete"
} else if (pooled_mean < 22) {
    "MNAR"
} else if (pooled_observed > length(pooled_values) / 2) {
    "MAR"
} else {
    "insufficient"
}

vegfa_states <- fit$classifications[
    fit$classifications$feature == "VEGFA",
    c("condition", "observed_count", "sample_count", "mean_intensity", "state")
]
vegfa_states <- vegfa_states[
    match(unique(condition), vegfa_states$condition),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
]
pooled_comparison <- rbind(
    data.frame(
        scope = "Pooled original samples",
        observed_count = pooled_observed,
        sample_count = length(pooled_values),
        mean_intensity = pooled_mean,
        state = pooled_state
    ),
    data.frame(
        scope = paste(vegfa_states$condition, "condition"),
        observed_count = vegfa_states$observed_count,
        sample_count = vegfa_states$sample_count,
        mean_intensity = vegfa_states$mean_intensity,
        state = vegfa_states$state
    )
)
knitr::kable(
    pooled_comparison,
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Scope", "Observed", "Samples", "Mean intensity", "State")
)

vegfa_status <- fit$feature_status[
    fit$feature_status$feature == "VEGFA",
    ,
    drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(
    identical(pooled_state, "insufficient"),
    identical(
        vegfa_states$state[
            match(c("control", "K63"), vegfa_states$condition)
        ],
        c("MNAR", "complete")
    ),
    isTRUE(vegfa_status$retained)
)
```

Pooling produces three observations from six samples. The mean is above the
cutoff, but there is no strict observed majority, so the feature becomes
`insufficient` and would be dropped. Condition-aware classification instead
records the control block as `MNAR`, the K63-linked block as `complete`, and
retains the affinity-enrichment on/off feature.

## Result components

- `data` - retained rows in the input representation, with recorded rescue
    values inserted.
- `classifications` - one row per feature and condition, with the values used
    for classification, the assigned state, and the retention decision.
- `groups` - retained `MNAR`, `MAR`, `complete`, and `MAR_or_complete` feature
    names for each condition.
- `feature_status` - one retention decision for every original feature.
- `cutoffs`, `cutoff_diagnostics` - condition boundaries, how they were chosen,
    method details, and warnings.
- `profiles` - feature statistics, the density grid, and smoothing details.
- `seed_log` - a record of each artificial rescue value, including rescues on
    features later dropped.
- `groups_by_sample` - aligned condition label for every output sample.
- `call` - the matched call used to create the result.

# The stored missingness profile

For each condition, ImputeFinder estimates missing and complete feature-mean
density curves on one intensity grid. If `n_1 f_1(x)` is the count-weighted
density for blocks with missing values and `n_0 f_0(x)` is the corresponding
density for complete blocks, the displayed profile is

```text
                n_1 f_1(x)
p_missing(x) = -------------------------
                n_1 f_1(x) + n_0 f_0(x)
```

This is the local proportion of incomplete feature blocks, not the average
fraction of missing samples. The feature statistics, grid, bandwidth, class
counts, warnings, and cutoff details are stored in the result. Plotting uses
those stored values directly.

```{r stored-profile}
fit$profiles$control$metadata[c("class_counts", "bandwidth", "kernel")]
head(
    fit$profiles$control$grid[
        , c("intensity", "missing_proportion", "supported")
    ]
)
```

```{r manual-profile, fig.cap=manual_profile_caption}
plot_missingness(fit, "control")
```

This seven-protein extract is selected to show classification rules, not to
estimate the full study profile. Its curve illustrates the stored profile,
manual cutoff, and rescue value, but it is too small for automatic selection or
scientific interpretation of the transition.

# Automatic cutoffs

Manual cutoffs are useful when domain knowledge or a predeclared analysis fixes
the boundary. With `cutoffs = NULL`, the default, ImputeFinder searches each
incomplete condition's profile for the lower, right-hand boundary of its main
downward transition. Conditions with no missing observations need no cutoff. A
partial named vector is also valid; automatic selection fills only the omitted
conditions.

The deterministic synthetic matrix below contains two clear but different
transitions. It uses a fixed mix of incomplete and complete features so the
vignette gives the same result every time it is built.

```{r automatic-data}
make_condition <- function(n, left, right, score_offset = 0L) {
    index <- seq_len(n)
    means <- qnorm((index - 0.5) / n, mean = 12.5, sd = 2.4)
    score <- (((index + score_offset) * 104729) %% 1000003) / 1000003
    ramp <- pmin(pmax((right - means) / (right - left), 0), 1)
    missing_probability <- 1 - (1 - 0.05) * (1 - 0.68 * ramp)
    missing <- score < missing_probability

    block <- matrix(rep(means, 4L), nrow = n)
    block[cbind(which(missing), rep(4L, sum(missing)))] <- NA_real_
    block
}

feature_count <- 200L
automatic_x <- cbind(
    make_condition(feature_count, left = 10.2, right = 11),
    make_condition(feature_count, left = 13.2, right = 14, score_offset = 37L)
)
rownames(automatic_x) <- sprintf("protein_%04d", seq_len(feature_count))
colnames(automatic_x) <- paste0("automatic_sample_", seq_len(ncol(automatic_x)))
automatic_condition <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4)
```

```{r automatic-fit}
automatic_fit <- classify_missingness(
    automatic_x,
    group = automatic_condition
)
round(automatic_fit$cutoffs, 3)
vapply(
    automatic_fit$cutoff_diagnostics,
    function(diagnostic) diagnostic$source,
    character(1)
)
automatic_fit$cutoff_diagnostics$A$method
```

```{r automatic-profile, fig.cap=automatic_profile_caption}
plot_missingness(automatic_fit, "A")
```

An automatic estimate is returned only when there are enough complete and
incomplete features, enough support across the intensity range, a decreasing
missingness trend, and a clear transition. Flat, missing-only, sparse, or
ambiguous profiles raise a condition-specific `imputefinder_cutoff_error` with
the profile and diagnostic attached. Complete-only conditions need no cutoff.
Inspect the stored profile and supply a named manual cutoff when automatic
estimation fails.

# Filtered data and downstream branches

`fit$data` contains only retained features and includes their logged rescue
anchors. `seed_log` also audits pre-filter rescues on features later dropped.
`fit$groups` divides the retained rows independently within each condition into
`MNAR`, `MAR`, `complete`, and the combined `MAR_or_complete` group.

The intended order is:

1. classify the unnormalised log2 matrix;
2. normalise the entire returned `fit$data` object with the method chosen for
    the experiment;
3. split samples by `fit$groups_by_sample`;
4. within each condition, apply an MNAR method only to its `MNAR` rows and a
    MAR method only to its `MAR_or_complete` rows;
5. recombine conditions in original sample order.

The following code performs the split and stops before normalisation or
imputation, because those choices depend on the analysis and are not
ImputeFinder dependencies.

```{r downstream-branches}
split_condition <- function(result, condition_name) {
    samples <- names(result$groups_by_sample)[
        result$groups_by_sample == condition_name
    ]
    condition_data <- result$data[, samples, drop = FALSE]

    list(
        MNAR = condition_data[
            result$groups[[condition_name]]$MNAR,
            ,
            drop = FALSE
        ],
        MAR_or_complete = condition_data[
            result$groups[[condition_name]]$MAR_or_complete,
            ,
            drop = FALSE
        ]
    )
}

downstream <- lapply(names(fit$groups), function(condition_name) {
    split_condition(fit, condition_name)
})
names(downstream) <- names(fit$groups)

vapply(downstream, function(branch) nrow(branch$MNAR), integer(1))
vapply(downstream, function(branch) nrow(branch$MAR_or_complete), integer(1))
c(
    VEGFA_in_control_MNAR = "VEGFA" %in% rownames(downstream$control$MNAR),
    VEGFA_in_K63_MAR_or_complete =
        "VEGFA" %in% rownames(downstream$K63$MAR_or_complete)
)
```

## An illustrative routing manifest

Suppose the analysis plan assigns an MNAR-aware method to low-intensity blocks,
a MAR-aware method to supported incomplete blocks, and no replacement to
complete blocks. The selected algorithms remain external to ImputeFinder. The
classification table can express that plan as a condition-specific manifest.

```{r routing-manifest}
manifest_features <- c("VEGFA", "UBE2I", "MED20")
routing_manifest <- fit$classifications[
    fit$classifications$retained &
        fit$classifications$feature %in% manifest_features,
    c("feature", "condition", "observed_count", "missing_count", "state")
]
routing_manifest <- routing_manifest[
    order(
        match(routing_manifest$feature, manifest_features),
        match(routing_manifest$condition, unique(condition))
    ),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
]
rownames(routing_manifest) <- NULL

pipeline_actions <- c(
    MNAR = "send to the MNAR branch",
    MAR = "send to the MAR branch",
    complete = "carry forward unchanged"
)
routing_manifest$pipeline_action <- unname(
    pipeline_actions[as.character(routing_manifest$state)]
)
knitr::kable(
    routing_manifest,
    col.names = c("Feature", "Condition", "Observed", "Missing", "State", "Action")
)
```

```{r routing-manifest-check, include=FALSE}
vegfa_route <- routing_manifest[
    routing_manifest$feature == "VEGFA",
    ,
    drop = FALSE
]
stopifnot(
    identical(as.character(vegfa_route$state), c("MNAR", "complete")),
    identical(
        vegfa_route$pipeline_action,
        c("send to the MNAR branch", "carry forward unchanged")
    )
)
```

The manifest sends `VEGFA` to the MNAR branch only for control samples. Its
three measured K63-linked values pass through unchanged. `UBE2I` enters the MAR
branch for controls and passes through the K63-linked branch unchanged. `MED20`
passes through the control branch unchanged and enters the K63-linked MAR
branch.

After branch outputs are recombined, `VEGFA` remains available to an enrichment
comparison model. A pooled classifier would have dropped it before
normalisation or imputation. The manifest records each block's state and
destination, while `fit$classifications` retains the supporting evidence.
Together they support review and reproducible reruns.

Complete blocks need no replacement. Grouping them with MAR rows supplies a
single non-MNAR branch while preserving each explicit `complete` state in the
classification table.

# `SummarizedExperiment` input

A `SummarizedExperiment` uses the same matrix core. Select the condition column
explicitly and name the assay whenever the object contains more than one. The
returned `data` preserves the representation, unselected assays, row and column
metadata, and sample order while filtering rows and replacing only the selected
assay with the seed-modified values.

```{r summarized-experiment}
se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(log2_intensity = x),
    colData = data.frame(
        condition = condition,
        row.names = colnames(x)
    )
)
fit_se <- classify_missingness(
    se,
    group_col = "condition",
    assay = "log2_intensity",
    cutoffs = c(control = 22, K63 = 22)
)
identical(
    SummarizedExperiment::assay(fit_se$data, "log2_intensity"),
    fit$data
)
```

# Limitations

- The cutoff is a model assumption. Biology, acquisition, and preprocessing can
    produce patterns without one descending intensity transition.
- Automatic breakpoint selection needs both incomplete and complete features.
    When the data do not support a clear transition, use a manual cutoff.
- Arithmetic means are sensitive to strong observations by design.
- Rescue anchors are artificial values. Preserve `seed_log` with the analysis
    and assess their influence downstream.
- Classification is heuristic. ImputeFinder does not prove mechanisms, choose
    an imputation algorithm, or validate the final biological analysis.

The test suite covers intensity-independent MAR,
intensity-dependent MNAR, condition-specific on/off features, several group
sizes and cutoffs, rescue seeds, and name permutations. These tests cover those
cases but do not establish performance for every proteomics experiment.
